item.title: Sight Loss Does Not Make Someone an Incomplete Person
item.description:
Bias

Sight Loss Does Not Make Someone an Incomplete Person

The paradox of independence: We must depend on others to act independently.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Culturally acquired stereotypes affect how visually impaired people see themselves and are seen by others.
  • Help that seems ordinary for sighted people often is interpreted as evidence of dependency in blind people.
  • Giving and receiving care and assistance are central features of being human.

Nadine, a research participant in a study on blindness, said that using a white cane in public often made her the center of attention. She explained: “…it’s difficult because sometimes you don’t want everyone to look at you when you walk into a room. Sometimes you just want to sneak in and go … I just want to blend in” (Konrad, 2021).

The white cane attracts the attention of sighted people because it signifies blindness, which evokes their fear about their own vulnerability and their curiosity about people they may rarely encounter in daily life (Paterson, 2013; Garland-Thomson, 2006).

The irony is that this attention-grabbing symbol of blindness often obscures the individuality of those using it, thereby transforming unique cane users into faceless ciphers of disability. As one blind woman put it: “I'm invisible. …Even in a room full of 100 people, I feel like I'm not seen” (Szilva, 2025, p. 63). The person disappears behind the white cane because, in the eyes of others, their disability is the essence of who they are. In fact, others tend to assume that the blind person’s disability explains their personality, motives, and behaviors (Nario-Redmond, 2020).

A bustling city street filled with various pedestrians and cyclists, with a tall dark building in the back. The crowd is at middle distance from the camera, so distinguishing features are largely lost.
Source: Sebastiaan Stam / Pexels

In this post, I will explore how the use of culturally acquired assumptions to interpret and evaluate the behaviors of visually impaired adults complicates how they view themselves and how they respond to sight loss.

Stereotypes and Internalized Stigma

The onset of sight loss most often occurs in middle age or after (Brinks et al., 2019; NHS England, 2024). The radical changes brought about by sight loss usually trigger an extended period of depression and anxiety, as people gradually make the journey from sightedness to blindness (Nyman et al., 2012). To forestall fully arriving at that destination, they may try to pass as sighted for as long as possible (Thurston, 2024).

Eventually, most people experiencing sight loss face reality, and some take advantage of services that teach the nonvisual skills needed to function effectively in their daily lives, despite limited availability (Kaldenberg et al., 2023). Learning to navigate the world with a white cane is perhaps the nonvisual skill most closely linked to feelings of shame, inferiority, and loss of identity (Berndtsson, 2025). When Alice began to use a cane, she described herself as almost subhuman:

When you have a disability, you’re not a whole person.…[That’s] what gives you this nagging feeling that somehow you don’t have the same human dignity, you’ve become a little less, a little lower, a little… well, you’re not a whole, complete person. (Berndtsson, 2025).

What might Alice have meant when she stated that she is not “a whole, complete person”? She likely was referring to what her culture has taught her about blindness and blind people. In childhood, we are exposed to and begin to learn stereotypic beliefs about a variety of social groups, including racial, gender, and disability groups (Devine, 1989; Farago et al., 2019).

People experiencing sight loss and other disabling impairments often view themselves and are viewed by others through the lens of cultural stereotypes that mark them as inferior and defective (Nario-Redmond, 2010, 2020; Ricker, 2023). The white cane is a powerful symbol of blindness that reminds its users of these stereotypic beliefs. The stereotypes characterize people with severe visual impairments as dependent, incompetent, and helpless.

A person is said to have “internalized stigma” when they have learned the stereotypes and use them to evaluate themselves (see Goffman, 1963). These stereotypic beliefs emphasize dependency, which suggests what might be meant by not being “a whole, complete person.” The majority of cultures in Western societies promote an ideal that may be called the “individualistic self” (Cushman, 1995; Markus & Kitayama, 1991).

Four students and an older teacher crouch in the soil, gathered around a patch of grass. The students are looking at a rock that the teacher is holding in one hand, poised as if explaining something to them.
Source: Hillebrand Steve / Pixnio

This ideal views the self as an internal center of agency: the maker and implementer of decisions that require no help from others. The individualistic self consists of a unique combination of elements that underlie our actions: traits, abilities, values, preferences, and desires.

The self is considered to be “bounded”: It is contained within the mind/body, and is presumed to be the primary determinant of our actions. The self, in essence, is assumed to stand alone in choosing goals and directing actions to achieve them. Thus, in this view, a whole, complete person exhibits total self-sufficiency, self-reliance, and autonomy.

Alice is not alone in thinking that reduced independence, understood as a reduced ability to perform tasks without help, somehow reduces one’s worth and dignity. A participant in another study lamented his lost independence: “I was independent all my life, I've done everything by myself … I now have to rely on other people to help in many, many ways” (cited in Enoch et al., 2025, p. 1121).

Some researchers and disability scholars argue for a shift towards encouraging interdependence rather than independence as a goal for adapting well to blindness and low vision.

Dependence, Independence, and Interdependence

Kenneth Jernigan, who served for years as the president of the National Federation of the Blind (NFB), gave a speech in 1993 in which he explained to some student critics why he used a sighted guide at the 1992 NFB convention. He stated that, when his mind was occupied with planning and completing tasks, depending on someone to guide him allowed him to concentrate on important matters.

Eva Feder Kittay, a philosopher of disability ethics, has questioned the ideal of the independent self. She has argued that no one is truly independent. Everyone, whether they are disabled or nondisabled, relies on “invisible” networks of supportive relationships that help them with daily tasks (Gesser & Fietz, 2021).

In his 1993 address, Jernigan provided an example that illustrated the importance of this publicly invisible support system in the lives of people who would seem to embody the cultural ideal of the independent, self-reliant person. Lamar Alexander, the Secretary of Education, spoke at the previous year’s convention. Alexander had an assistant arrive a day ahead of time to take care of arrangements. He picked Alexander up at the airport, accompanied him to the meeting room, walked with him to the stage, met him after the talk, and drove him to the airport. Alexander was fully capable of doing all those things without help, but he just did not have the time. Jernigan mused: “If the Secretary had been blind, I wonder if somebody would have said, ‘Just look! He's not independent. He has to have a sighted person with him at all times.’”

For Kittay, needing assistance does not make us incomplete humans or unworthy of human dignity. Needing assistance and giving assistance to others is what being human is all about: They are central features of the human condition.

Furthermore, it is unclear, to say the least, how one can classify requests for help as:

  • indicating dependence when made by disabled people
  • consistent with independence when made by nondisabled people

Ultimately, the argument for this double standard seems to be an invalid one:

  • disabled people are incompetent and, therefore, their requests for help indicate dependency
  • nondisabled people are competent and, therefore, their requests for help do not indicate dependency

The stereotypes causing all the trouble hold a firm grasp on our thinking about disability. They have a powerful influence on how we view others and also on how we view ourselves. Their stubborn refusal to yield to reason helps to explain why adapting to disabling impairments such as blindness can be a lifelong process.

item.title: It's Time We Remember the Great Forgetting
item.description:
Evolutionary Psychology

It's Time We Remember the Great Forgetting

The clock is ticking faster, and the way home is something we already know.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Hunter-gatherers built a stone monument before farms existed—a clue to what first drew strangers together.
  • The walls we built for shelter and status slowly became a prison, separating us from nature and each other.
  • Feeling anxious and lonely in a hyperconnected world may reflect how far we’ve drifted from who we are.

Why are we here? What is our purpose? How shall we live? We humans have probably been asking these big questions for as long as we have been human. Perhaps what makes us most human is that we all possess a consciousness that can ask them.

We understand our world through stories. Without meaning to, we built a prison for ourselves, and remembering who we truly are is what sets us free.

Here’s a Story of Us, and it begins with the Great Forgetting.

The Great Forgetting

In his novel Ishmael, Daniel Quinn describes two stories humans have lived by. In one, the world belongs to us. In the other, we belong to the world. For nearly all of our history, we lived the second story. When we began to farm and settle down roughly 10,000 to 12,000 years ago, we started living the first.

So we moved indoors. We built houses, villages, and cities. Walls kept out the cold and the predators, and those dreaded “others.” They also kept us from seeing that we are part of nature, not apart from it. Slowly, our walls became a prison of separateness.

In a later book, The Story of B, Quinn named what happened next: the Great Forgetting. Our culture lost touch with the long human story that came before it, as if humanity began where civilization did.

A Shared Quest for the Divine

Think about the last time you stood under a sky full of stars. Most of us have felt very small and very lucky at the same moment, an awe that is both humbling and connecting. How did we get here? What are we part of?

For a long time, the story of civilization ran in one direction. First came farming, then villages, and eventually temples. Göbekli Tepe threw that story into question. About 11,500 years ago, people who lived by hunting and gathering began raising enormous carved stone pillars on that hilltop, some more than 18 feet tall and weighing 10 tons or more. Archaeologist Klaus Schmidt put it simply: “First came the temple, then the city.”

That idea is mind-boggling. The quest to understand ourselves and commune with the divine may have helped lead us into civilization, which in turn made it easy to forget who we are.

Excavators have since found signs that people lived there, too, so Schmidt’s famous sequence is now debated. As psychologist Tracy Henley puts it, calling Göbekli Tepe a temple is “likely accurate, but perhaps also misleading.” For its builders, the line between sacred and ordinary was almost certainly blurred. That may be the first thing we forgot.

How the Walls Went Up

As people settled, stored food, and claimed land, leaving got harder, and the stories that once taught a band to share could be retold to explain why some deserved more. Over thousands of years, we built walls that protected us but also divided us, the haves from the have-nots, and all of us from nature.

The ladder of success in our ancient hunter-gatherer tribes was a step stool. At most, we might earn a little extra respect in our mostly egalitarian band, and life was hard enough that our end could come at any time. As we entered civilization, the ladder of success grew from large houses to castles to the tops of golden skyscrapers. As Lord Acton wrote in 1887, “Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.” The key word is “tends.”

Nobody needs to be the villain here. We are victims of our own success. The drive for status lives in all of us. But when we left our tribes and nature to build civilization, the mismatch began to widen.

Over time, we stop noticing the walls at all. Winston Churchill put it this way in 1943: “We shape our buildings and afterwards our buildings shape us.” Not only that, we’ve forgotten that our true home had no walls at all.

Today we are running god-like software on Stone Age hardware. I call this Accelerating Evolutionary Mismatch. It's the Great Forgetting made visible.

For most of our species’ history, the world changed slowly enough for us to keep up. Now it can transform within a single lifetime, while our brains still expect the old one. We feel the gap in small moments, like a parent watching a game on a phone while their own child plays fifteen feet away. None of this means we’re broken. We’re having a natural response to an increasingly unnatural world.
Source: Mike Brooks/Claude

And the clock is speeding up. On that graph, the time between our great revolutions shrinks from hundreds of thousands of years to a matter of decades.

That gap creates a prison that entraps us. Many of us feel anxious without a clear reason, overwhelmed by the sense that we can’t keep up with an accelerating treadmill. We feel lonely despite, or perhaps because of, our digital connectedness.

The Buddha taught that attachment is the root of suffering. Now, with our smartphones, we are attached to something we didn’t evolve to even hold. The walls that once sheltered us now imprison us.

The Great Remembering

Let’s reconsider the Garden of Eden. After Adam and Eve eat the fruit, “the eyes of them both were opened.” Perhaps that is the moment we became fully aware—conscious—of ourselves and began to wonder how we got here. With that awakening came the knowledge that we die and feed the trees. In the traditional reading, we were cast out of the garden.

Perhaps we walked out of the Garden on our own, seeking to connect with one another and find answers to the Big Questions. In seeking those answers, we left the Garden and then forgot where we came from. In trying to find our lives, we lost them.

“We are here to awaken from the illusion of our separateness.” –Thich Nhat Hanh

The first awakening, in the Garden, made us aware of ourselves. The next awakening is remembering that we all share the same home. As fellow Homo sapiens, we have always been part of the natural world.

Our fractured but interconnected world needs a story big enough to leave no one outside. I’m not talking about a new dogma. Our differences are real, and some are worth arguing about. But they aren't worth hating and killing one another over.

I don’t think we need a new story at all. As Quinn advocated, we need a Great Remembering.

Who we are is who we were.

“Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing, there is a field. I’ll meet you there.” –Rumi

We built the walls and forgot the Field was always our home.

We began our existence in nature, in a Garden, if you will. Perhaps the Field and the Garden are the same place, and the way back home is simply to remember. Long before anyone had the language of evolution, our greatest spiritual teachers had a simpler word for one human family. They called us neighbors.

We’ve all been in the Field, even if only for a moment. Think of the last time a storm or a power outage turned strangers into neighbors. Nobody asked who anyone voted for. For a little while, the walls weren’t there.

We built the walls together, so we’ll have to take them down together. When enough of us remember that we’re neighbors, we can connect and cooperate.

Our corridor to a thriving future is as narrow as our divisions and as wide as our cooperation.

Each line through the corridor stands for a possible future. When risks are shared, racing one another for advantage tends to leave everyone less safe, while working together keeps more futures open, including some no single group could reach alone. Nobody knows exactly how this turns out. We do not need to know the ending to take responsibility for the next chapter.
Source: Mike Brooks/ChatGPT

We’re all neighbors in an interconnected world. Remembering who we truly are sets us free to love our neighbors as ourselves, and the Golden Rule, treating others as we wish to be treated, is how we practice that love.

Truth must be lived, just as oxygen must be breathed, to matter.

Our future will be revealed by the choices we make now.

item.title: Why We Can’t Go It Alone
item.description:
Happiness

Why We Can’t Go It Alone

How happiness requires people, not Amazon packages.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • The biggest influence on happiness is being around people and getting along with them.
  • Your social circle needs to consist of more than just your houseplants and a cat.
  • Our ability to adapt to fellow humans, and all the ups and downs relationships cause, is key to contentment.
  • The happiness formula might be the people right next to you.

If a formula for achieving happiness existed, most of us would be following it to the letter. It would also be a global money-making business, marketed in every country. You could buy it online, and perhaps it would even be taught in schools and universities. But happiness doesn’t have a blueprint. It can’t be ordered with free two-day shipping.

So, what is the origin of happiness? Perhaps it comes from finding meaning and purpose in our short existence? Or pursuing a fulfilling career? Embracing spirituality? Is it a result of having love in our lives? Or some other source?

These days, it seems that most happiness-boosting approaches point towards building up your individuality and focusing on you. For decades, we have all been marinating in the self-help ethos that prescribes the inward shift to the self as the only way to foster happiness. Social media, especially, drives that pop psychology viewpoint.

But experts tell us that the biggest influence on happiness (not necessarily the exact cause of it) is being around people and getting along with them. It’s also in the value of our family ties, our intimate partnerships, and our friendships. Therefore, if you are planning to outlive everyone that you know, your social circle needs to consist of more than just your houseplants and a cat. You may need to mix it up a little and find a few human souls.

The 2023 book, The Good Life: Lessons from the World's Longest Scientific Study of Happiness, underlines how significantly our well-being is linked to our human relationships. For example, one of the many studies found that “the people who were the most satisfied in their relationships at age 50 were the healthiest (mentally and physically) at age 80." In other words, healthy relationships and strong bonds help us not only to prosper, but live longer too.

The Power of Human Interaction

Our ability to adapt to fellow humans and learn how to deal with all the ups and downs that relationships cause is key to contentment. When we engage with other people as our imperfect selves, and we feel safe and accepted, it refutes the illusion that happiness lies only within the self. This speaks to what so many of us consider one of life's decisive objectives: finding someone who embraces us for who we genuinely are. If we are lucky enough to find that, it makes life feel pretty good.

Also, we all know the exceptional joy of connecting with like-minded souls—those who mirror our experiences and share our passions. Sharing moments and activities with others not only reduces loneliness and breeds a sense of universality, but it also makes us feel secure. Having people who can bear witness to our milestones, achievements, and even our sorrows is invaluable.

So even if you like being alone, as humans, we are and have always been social creatures that need each other for survival. We didn’t evolve for thousands of years in a vacuum. Plus, research also shows that in the long run, engaging with others and hopefully finding people to love gives our lives the most significance. It also gives us our identity by reflecting back to us our own humanity.

Psychoanalyst Stephen A. Mitchell, from his book Relational Concepts in Psychoanalysis: Integration, said, “We live in a relational matrix. The person is comprehensible only within this tapestry of relationships, past or present.” In other words, the quality of our relationships clarifies us. Without them, we are inadequate, searching in the dark for a likeness we can only find in our fellow humans. Perhaps when we find the likeness, we find the joy.

Hence, stop looking for the undisclosed blueprint and discover why the ultimate happy formula may not be a solo project—it might be the people right next to you.

But for those of you who are less inclined to place a premium on close and familial connections, here are a few other important factors to happiness that cannot be denied or ignored. Acknowledging and practicing these sustainable aspects of living could additionally help make you more content on a regular basis.

For example, having gratitude for what you have. Secondly, connecting to your own interpretation of God or a higher power. And thirdly, having a sense of purpose and goals.

Look at happiness as a series of actions to exercise every day, not a destination to reach or something you can add to your shopping cart. Remember, humans are not built for separateness; you will be better off sharing some parts of your life with others. Therefore, don’t look at it as an “all or nothing” thing. Find the nuance, the gray area where you can connect and spend time with others without compromising your “alone” time. Isolation is the new smoking.

item.title: What If Nothing Is Wrong With You?
item.description:
Self-Esteem

What If Nothing Is Wrong With You?

It's possible to awaken from the trance of unworthiness.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Psychologist Tara Brach calls the belief that something is wrong with oneself “the trance of unworthiness.”
  • Self-worth is shaped by a person's earliest relationships, and those beliefs can be unlearned.
  • Mindfulness, self-compassion, self-understanding can help people begin to reconnect with their worth.
Source: AnnHannes/Pexels

In my nearly two decades as a therapist, I’ve sat with hundreds of people of all ages and backgrounds, and one thing has become clear: By adulthood, feeling inherently lovable and worthy seems to be the exception rather than the rule.

The quiet belief that “something is fundamentally wrong with me” is a burden so many of us carry as we move through life, often without even realizing it. Psychologist and Buddhist meditation teacher Tara Brach describes this as living under “the trance of unworthiness.” It may sound like:

  • “I’m not smart enough.”
  • “I’m not talented enough.”
  • “I don’t deserve this.”

But we don’t start out this way. “Babies don't wonder whether they deserve to be seen, connected with, or held,” says Jackie Ourman, LMHC, couples and individual therapist at Values Aligned Therapy and founder of Social Connection Collective. “Our earliest relationships teach us about our value through the ways the people who are supposed to care for us respond to our needs.”

What we learned, we can begin to unlearn.

5 Ways to Connect to Your Inherent Worth

Consider these practices to help you awaken from the trance of unworthiness.

1. Recognize you're in the trance of unworthiness.

When we are caught in the trance, deeply rooted negative beliefs can feel like indisputable facts. Ourman encourages her clients to notice that what they are experiencing is a thought, not necessarily a fact.

“There’s a difference,” Ourman says, “between saying, ‘I’m not enough’ and saying, ‘I’m having the thought that I’m not enough.’ This creates a little distance from our thoughts so we don’t automatically believe everything our minds tell us.”

Simply noticing that we are in the midst of a self-critical inner monologue is a powerful act in itself. That is mindfulness: observing thoughts without judgment and without being swept away by them.

2. Take the sacred pause.

In her book, Radical Acceptance, Brach describes a practice she calls the “sacred pause,” drawing on Buddhist teachings. The next time you notice yourself spiraling, stop and take a breath. Notice what’s happening in your body and which thoughts have arrived. Resist the urge to fix, explain, or dismiss what you feel. Then ask yourself:

“What does my heart truly long for in this moment?”

Not “what would make me more impressive or more acceptable to others.” Simply, “What does your heart truly long for right now?” Ask again, and wait.

The pause gives us an opportunity to listen more deeply and reconnect with our soul voice, the one within us that knows what we truly need.

3. Send compassion to the little you who took on the burden of “not good enough.”

For many of us, it's easier to offer compassion to our child selves than to our present selves. If this resonates, try this exercise.

Find the most endearing photo you can of yourself as a child. One that evokes warmth or tenderness. Spend some time looking into the little one’s eyes. See their desire to belong, or their simple wish to be loved. Then ask yourself:

What did that little one need to hear? What did they need to know about themselves? Perhaps they needed to know that their needs weren’t too much, or that they weren’t responsible for the things that happened to them.

4. See yourself through the eyes of those who love you.

When we’re caught in the trance of unworthiness, our view of ourselves can become remarkably narrow. We fixate on our perceived flaws and overlook the qualities others see so clearly.

Think of a person who genuinely loves you; someone who sees you with affection. What might they say about you? What qualities would they notice that you routinely overlook? What would they remind you of when you are convinced that you have nothing worthwhile to offer?

This is not about depending on others’ approval to feel okay. It is about recognizing that our self-perception isn’t always reliable and never fully captures who we are.

5. Understand where the beliefs came from.

When we begin to understand how our negative beliefs originated, we can extend compassion to the younger version of ourselves who was simply trying to make sense of their experiences.

“I think it's important to acknowledge and validate those early experiences while also recognizing that the conclusions someone drew about themselves may not be true,” says Ourman. “For many people, the work is less about building worth from scratch and more about finding their way back to it.”

A Gentle Invitation

You don’t have to believe you are worthy overnight. These old beliefs may have been with you for a long time, but with patience, they can begin to loosen. Start with one small practice, whichever one speaks to you.

May you be kind to yourself and find your way back to the worth that was always there.

item.title: Why Do We Love Some Accents and Hate Others?
item.description:
Bias

Why Do We Love Some Accents and Hate Others?

The way we hear accents can be rooted in hidden prejudices.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • A person's reactions to accents often reveals more about their own prejudices than the way people speak.
  • No accent is inherently more intelligent, attractive, or better than another.
  • Accent bias can have serious real-world consequences, affecting how people are perceived and treated.

We all have personal opinions about certain accents. Some make us swoon, while others make us cringe. They seem to inspire remarkably strong reactions for something as ordinary as the way a person pronounces their words.

To many people’s ears, a French accent might sound sophisticated and seductive, while a German accent is sometimes described as harsh or angry. A British accent may suggest refinement and education, but depending on where in Britain it comes from, it could also attract assumptions about someone’s intelligence or social class.

However, our reactions to accents often reveal more about our own prejudices than the people speaking. And these judgments aren't harmless: Accent bias can affect how people are perceived and treated.

Everyone Has an Accent. Yes, Even You!

An accent is the way we pronounce words that is influenced by our regional and social backgrounds. Everyone has one, although some people mistakenly believe they speak without an accent and that it’s everyone else who has one.

Accents carry powerful social associations and biases. (Stollznow, 2026) Perhaps the best-known example in British English is Received Pronunciation (RP), better known as the Queen’s English (now the King’s English) or BBC English. Popularized through the BBC’s newsreaders and presenters in the 1920s, this accent became associated with education, wealth, authority, and social privilege. To many people, it still sounds like the voice of someone who knows what they’re talking about.

But not all accents enjoy this same prestige. The Southern U.S. accent is sometimes unfairly associated with a lack of education, intelligence, or sophistication, reflecting longstanding stereotypes about the American South. Yet such perceptions depend on the context. In some communities, a Southern drawl might signal warmth, friendliness, authenticity, and regional pride. The same accent that one listener dismisses as unsophisticated might be valued by another as a marker of identity and belonging. Linguists call this covert prestige. This is the social value attached to ways of speaking that might not be considered prestigious by wider society, but are highly prized within particular communities.

Accent prejudice can also reflect much deeper social inequalities. African American English, for example, has long been stigmatized through racist stereotypes associating its speakers with laziness, poor education, and criminality. (Barrett, et al., 2022) These judgments have little to do with the dialect itself and everything to do with the prejudices faced by this group of people. Within this community, however, African American English is an important marker of identity, solidarity, and cultural pride. Its influence on jazz, R&B, hip hop, and popular culture also demonstrates its considerable cultural prestige beyond the community.

The Language of Love (and Hate)

Our reactions to accents aren’t always about social class or race. Sometimes, we simply decide subjectively that certain languages sound more beautiful while others sound unpleasant (Crystal, 2014). For instance, French has a longstanding reputation as the language of love. Its associations with romance, fashion, fine dining, and literature have helped cement its image as elegant and sophisticated. Its rhythm, nasal vowels, and soft consonants contribute to the impression of musicality. There’s even a popular notion that everything sounds better in French, including insults. In The Matrix Reloaded, the Merovingian declares, “I have sampled every language. French is my favorite—a fantastic language, especially to curse with.” He then launches into a string of obscenities. It’s an unconventional endorsement, but it captures the seductive reputation that French has acquired.

The German language often gets a less flattering reception. It’s regularly described as harsh, guttural, or aggressive. The Irish comedian Dylan Moran once joked that German “sounds like a typewriter eating tinfoil being kicked down the stairs.” Its consonant clusters and sharp sounds might contribute to this impression, but our reactions are also affected by cultural stereotypes. German speakers are sometimes portrayed as cold, rigid, and overly concerned with rules and order. Historical associations with World War II and Nazi Germany have also influenced negative perceptions of the language. These stereotypes have a long history. The 16th-century Holy Roman Emperor Charles V once said that he spoke Spanish to God, Italian to women, French to men, and German to his horse.

It’s Not the Accent

Of course, French isn’t inherently romantic, and German isn’t naturally angry. No accent is objectively more intelligent, attractive, or pleasant than any other. These impressions are learned, reinforced by cultural representations, historical associations, media portrayals, and even our own personal experiences with the accent.

What sounds sophisticated to one listener might sound pretentious to someone else. What sounds friendly and familiar to one person might sound provincial to another. These judgments can have serious real-world consequences. Accent prejudice can influence hiring decisions, education, healthcare and legal outcomes, social relationships, and how much credibility we give someone. We might like to think we’re judging people based on what they say, but sometimes we’re making up our minds before we’ve even heard their point of view.

Perhaps the next time we find ourselves admiring or disliking someone’s accent, it’s worth considering what we’re really responding to. Is it the sounds themselves, or the stories, stereotypes, and biases we’ve attached to them?

item.title: Measurability Bias, HR Tech, and Work: The Unholy Trinity
item.description:
Career

Measurability Bias, HR Tech, and Work: The Unholy Trinity

When the need to measure becomes more important than the need, nobody wins.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Measurability bias drives the investment and development of HR technology to focus on only half the field.
  • Hiring, training, performance management, and core HR (payroll, admin) receive the lion's share of resources.
  • Leadership, motivation, organizational development, and culture are harder to measure so get less attention.

In its very design, industrial/organizational (I/O) psychology (a.k.a. "psychology of work") reveals something nuanced and supremely relevant about what drives behavior in organizations.

Industrial psychology treats the individual as the unit of measure, while organizational psychology measures the group. The former tends to be measured quantitatively, while the latter tends to be measured qualitatively.

So, what falls on the “I” side (selection, training, performance management, core human resources [HR]) is very different than what falls on the “O” side (leadership, motivation, organizational development, culture).

From a technological investment point of view, “I” has a lot going for it. For starters, only quantitative data flows cleanly into a system of record, so there’s a built-in motivation for organizational use. But that’s not even the half of it.

Measure Twice, Cut Once

Measurability bias describes the tendency of people to prioritize easily quantifiable metrics over qualitative factors that are difficult, if not impossible, to measure.

It’s not hard to understand why. Easily quantifiable metrics require a lot less thinking and ostensibly provide a lot more certainty. (Of course, “ostensibly” is necessary because they’re so often applied incorrectly.)

Human beings hate uncertainty at a cellular level, and we often embrace whatever we can to reassure ourselves that we are making the right decision. This tendency is heightened in professional settings because the stakes are so high. We go out of our way to leverage quantitative data for guidance, cover, and reassurance.

That’s why “I” gets the prize, and it’s not hard to see why. According to analysis by 451 Research, less than 2 percent of sales of the $94 billion HR technology market goes to the qualitatively measured “O” constructs.

The same is true for investment. HRO Today tracked investment in 2025 and found that nearly all of the $3.75 billion went into the “I” side.

And where the technology and investment go, so goes the human attention.

As a result, constructs like leadership, motivation, and organizational culture receive comparably tiny resources and attention. Even something squarely on the “O” side like employee engagement, which had a brief run as the HR metric du jour, only did so because it offered a quantitative measure of a qualitative construct.

If the bias for easily quantifiable metrics creates a disincentive to pursue qualitative constructs through technology and investment, can we at least assume that the upside is that we’re making great decisions, grounded in data and analytics? Nope.

Oops, I Did It Again

What does the peer-reviewed research say about the efficacy of HR technology and investment on the “I” side of I/O psychology? There’s not a lot of it. What we do know isn’t promising.

Hiring? Research from Bauer and SHRM (2010) indicates that half of senior hires fail within 18 months, and that 50 percent of hourly workers leave within the first 120 days.

Training? A study by Saks and Belcourt (2006) found that two out of three trainees were not using the training one year later.

One could argue that HR technology has adopted these same practices and merely reproduced them at greater scale, as Capelli did in his HBR article (2019).

Performance management? Scullen, Mount, and Goff (2000) found that between 53 and 62 percent of variance in feedback is reflective of the feedback provider, not the feedback recipient. In other words, the feedback tells us more about the person providing it than the person receiving it. Kluger and DeNisi (1996) found that feedback actually harms performance more than a third of the time.

That research may be dated, but it reveals something fundamental about human behavior that performance management still fails to take into account.

There’s an ironic twist, to boot. What gets in the way of the efficacy of the heavily weighted technological investment in industrial psychology driven by measurement bias? Measurement bias.

What gets measured in selection? Volume of applications and time to fill. What doesn’t get measured? Outcomes. For training, it’s completion and satisfaction. And most performance management efforts have little to do with performance.

We don’t measure the outcomes of hiring decisions because it’s too hard to do and takes way too long. The same is true for training outcomes. By the time we know, we think (incorrectly) it’s too late to do anything about it. And performance management? The logical overriding motivation for managers is not to hurt anyone’s motivation moving forward, and that's not what performance management is designed to do.

Aye, Aye AI

Concerns about the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) on people and work are as well-founded as they are widespread. But they also overlook how AI can help us to be more human.

The ability to analyze qualitative data sets at a breakneck speed means that practitioners finally have access to the types of evidence that provide demonstrable proof of impact and return on investment (ROI).

Proper use of AI can tell us more about leadership, motivation, and culture at an organization than we have ever known. And it can do so in ways that support great decision-making, both strategically and tactically.

Our company is designing HR tools that can provide the benefits of psychological safety (surfacing truth) where it does not exist. We achieve this by summarizing anonymous qualitative data in real time, carefully framing the summary to avoid finger-pointing and surfacing the most productive steps forward.

We accelerate team decision-making by summarizing everyone’s opinion before the conversation begins, using pre-surfaced conflicting points of view as the starting point for discussions. We use AI to nudge people into creating better and more aligned goals across the organization. And now we can surface the way work really gets done through a combination of AI-document reviews and AI-assisted human-led interviews.

These are but a few examples of how AI can revolutionize HR and HR tech: by creating better sources of qualitative data. It may sound abstract, but the positive effect on work will be profound.

Yes, the impact that AI can have on the future of work is very scary. But interestingly, it also just might make the future of work way more human.

item.title: What Kids Won't Tell Their Parents
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

What Kids Won't Tell Their Parents

What kids hide, why they hide it, and how to get them talking.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Children hold back for reasons that make sense to them, including fear of our reaction and family reputation.
  • Young people who can’t disagree safely often comply on the surface and hide what they really do.
  • Side-by-side conversations and calm reactions to small news make bigger disclosures more likely.

November is a good month to be a child in the Gulf. The heat has broken, and families are outside in the evenings for the first time since spring. It is also the point in the school year when the novelty has worn off. Friendship groups have settled, and the first-term report cards are a few weeks away.

For many parents, this is when “How was school?” starts to get the same one-word answer every afternoon: "Fine."

Here in the Gulf, that answer can cover a lot. Our children attend demanding schools in a competitive environment. Their friendship groups shift every year as families arrive and leave, and many of them have been the new child more than once. They are navigating friendship politics and the pressure to do well, and much of it never comes up at home.

This is not unusual, and it is not a sign that something is wrong. Keeping some things private is a normal part of growing up. The more useful question is what leads children to open up.

Where Parents’ Knowledge Really Comes From

Two influential studies by Kerr and Stattin (2000) examined how parents come to know about their children’s lives. The common assumption was that parents who ask more questions and keep closer track know more. Instead, the researchers found that parents’ knowledge came mostly from what their children chose to tell them. Spontaneous disclosure, rather than tracking or questioning, predicted how much parents knew, and it was linked to better adjustment in the children themselves.

We cannot question our way into our children’s inner lives. We can only make it more likely that they will let us in.

Why Children Hold Back

Smetana and colleagues (2006, 2009) found that children’s reasons for keeping things to themselves vary. Some matters feel personal, and privacy is part of developing independence. Others are things children expect their parents to disapprove of, so they weigh the cost of our reaction against the relief of telling us.

In our part of the world, there is an additional layer. In my research with Arab families, honor and reputation came up again and again as issues that mattered to young people and their parents, and they were not well captured by the Western measures of family conflict available to us (Rasmi, Daly, & Chuang, 2014). Children in our communities learn early that some things reflect on the whole family and that awareness makes them more careful about what they bring home.

Younger children often do not have the words yet. A 9-year-old who feels left out at school rarely says so. Instead, her parents hear about her stomach ache on a Sunday evening.

Saying Yes and Doing Otherwise

One finding from my own work has stayed with me. When we asked young Arab Canadians how they handled disagreements with their parents, the most common approach was to oblige (i.e., to go along with what their parents wanted). On the surface, this looked like the least conflict of all. However, we found, in interviews with emerging adults, that obliging took two distinct forms: Some young people genuinely deferred to their parents, whereas others said yes to their parents’ faces and then quietly did what they had planned anyway (Rasmi, Daly, & Chuang, 2014).

That second group is the one parents need to think about. A child who has learned that disagreement is not safe at home keeps disagreeing but stops telling you about it.

What Makes the Difference

In a follow-up study, we interviewed young people about their relationships with their parents and found that the quality of the relationship shaped almost everything else (Rasmi, Chuang, & Hennig, 2017). Young people talked through their differences when the relationship was close, trusting, and marked by open communication. On the other hand, they withheld information to avoid conflict when they perceived the relationship to be distant or strictly hierarchical. In our quantitative research, a stronger parent–child relationship was also associated with less conflict at home (Rasmi, Chuang, & Hennig, 2015).

Smetana’s research points the same way. Adolescents disclose more to parents they experience as trusting and accepting. Children talk to the parents they feel safe with. That was true of the families I studied in Canada, and it is true of the families we see in Dubai.

How to Encourage Your Child to Open Up

  • Ask smaller questions. “How was your day?” invites one word. “Who did you sit with at lunch?” gives your child somewhere to start.

  • Talk side by side. Children share more when they are not being looked at directly, and this is the season for it. A walk on the beach after dinner gives you an hour with no screens and no eye contact. Bedtime works, too, when the lights are low.

  • Watch your reaction. Tilton-Weaver and colleagues (2010) found that when children met negative reactions after sharing something, they shared less afterward. Our response to the lost hoodie tells our children how we will respond to the bigger things.

  • Make disagreement safe. If your child can tell you they disagree and the conversation stays respectful, they are far more likely to tell you what is actually going on. You can hold your position and still let them voice theirs.

  • Let silence do some work. Children often circle a difficult topic before they land on it, and if we jump in too soon, they tend to retreat.

  • Notice what their body is saying. Stomach aches with no medical explanation can be a sign of something unsaid. So can a change in sleep or pulling away from things they used to enjoy. Several together, or any lasting more than a couple of weeks, are worth a gentle conversation and, if needed, a professional.

Privacy Is Not Secrecy

A child who keeps some things private while otherwise seeming like themselves is doing something healthy. A child who becomes withdrawn or unlike themselves alongside the silence may need more support. The goal is not to know everything, but to be the person your child comes to when it matters.

My colleagues Natalie Maaitah and Valen Valentine and I discussed this on a recent episode of our podcast, Thrive With Us. One idea stayed with me: Connection has to come before correction. Our children only tell us when they have learned that we are safe to tell.

November 20 is World Children’s Day, and its theme, in one form or another, is always listening to children. The cooler months give us more time together than any other part of the year. Some of it can go to smaller questions and to listening to the answers.

item.title: The Correlation Between Sports and Suicide
item.description:
Suicide

The Correlation Between Sports and Suicide

There’s a risk for players—and also for fans.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Suicides by professional athletes aren’t confined to football.
  • At least 77 former Major League Baseball players have killed themselves.
  • The success or failure of a sports team is related to suicides by the teams’ fans.

The list of professional athletes who have killed themselves is long. It includes all-pro football players Junior Seau, Mike Webster, and Jim Tyrer; “Miracle on Ice” hockey star Mark Pavelich; Olympic beach volleyball medalist Mike Whitmarsh; Olympic freestyle skiing medalist Jeret Peterson; Olympic women’s cycling medalist Kelly Catlin; pro golfer Erica Blasberg; Cy Young Award winner Mike Flanagan; Yankees pitcher Hideki Irabu; and Angels pitcher Donnie Moore.

Factors That Increase Athletes’ Suicide Risk

One reason why athletes have a high risk of suicide is that people who have enjoyed adulation and success throughout their young lives sometimes have a hard time adjusting when their playing days end. The roar of the crowd is gone, the adrenaline rush that accompanies top-level competition is no longer there, big paychecks most likely have ceased, locker room camaraderie is absent, and trainers and agents aren’t around to provide round-the-clock personal care. Most athletes who leave the game are still young by professional standards, whereas others in their 30s have begun to establish them­selves in long-term careers; athletes are just starting out and may not be prepared for life after sports.

According to one university researcher, 77 former Major League Baseball players have killed themselves. More than half were between their late 20s and late 40s, when their absence from the game was the most pronounced and future plans were uncertain, leading the researcher to recommend that MLB players receive counseling after they retire.[1]

Another factor is that many professional athletes leave the game with beat-up bodies. They were in peak physical shape when they first started playing, but overuse of joints and muscles plus injuries have taken a toll, mentally as well as physically. It’s hard to say goodbye to the limelight, but even harder sometimes to adjust to life afterward—chronic pain, decreased mobility, and—if they have suffered concussions—possible and permanent brain impairment.

In recent years, the results of studies on CTE—brain degeneration caused by repeated head trauma—have raised troubling concerns. At this time, there isn’t an accurate diagnostic test for CTE in living brains—it can only be found postmortem—but Chris Nowinski, a behavioral bio-scientist who played football in college, says that 99 percent of former NFL players whose brains have been examined posthumously have had CTE, and more than a few have died by suicide.[2]

Horse racing presents its own challenges. First and most obviously, it’s extremely dangerous. According to the president and CEO of the Jockey’s Guild, two jockeys die each year, on average, from racing, and 60 others are paralyzed. The concussions that jockeys get from falling off a horse at high speeds are as violent as the collisions of football players, and jockeys wear less protective gear. Add to this the challenge of maintaining a low weight, which results in eating disorders, plus frequent criticism from owners, trainers, and bettors, and it’s not surprising that jockeys suffer a variety of mental health issues. Three years ago, the horse racing world was stunned by the suicides of two jockeys. One of them was a friend of Mike Smith, who won the Triple Crown in 2018 at the age of 52 and is in the Racing Hall of Fame. Smith said that he knew other riders who killed themselves. “This is not all of a sudden just happening,” he said. “It’s been going on. You just never heard of it.”[3]

To date, only one female athlete has been diagnosed with CTE—a former Australian rules football player who played seven games in 2017, retired later that year, and killed herself in 2022 at age 28. Her family donated her brain to the Australian Sports Brain Bank, and the director there reported that he found “multiple CTE lesions.”[4] Here in the United States, two former World Cup stars, Brandi Chastain and Michelle Akers, have expressed public concern over memory-loss issues after they retired, and said that they will participate in a CTE study at Boston University.

The Link Between Sports Outcomes and Community Suicide Rates

Players and former players aren’t the only people at risk of suicide, however. Studies show that when a city’s most popular sports teams win a national championship, there is a temporary decline in the suicide rate. Conversely, after a loss, the rate goes up.

The U.S. men’s hockey team’s 1980 Olympic victory over the Soviet Union—the so-called “Miracle on Ice”—came at a time when the Iran hostage crisis had gone on for 111 days, and Russia’s invasion of Afghanistan was a month old. Millions of people in America had never seen a hockey game, didn’t know the rules or the names of any of the players, yet were glued to their TV sets and radios, cheering the home team to victory. It’s not surprising that the U.S. suicide rate was unusually low that day, February 22, 1980, compared with other February 22nds in the 20 years before and 20 years after.[5] (It may have been unusually high in the Soviet Union, although there are no data available to verify this.)

Suicide expert Thomas Joiner, who conducted that study, has conducted other studies that show a link between the success or failure of a sports team and suicide. For example, he found that fewer suicides occur on Sundays in America when the Super Bowl is played than on other Sundays during the year. Also, he determined that there is a correlation between the suicide rate and the national rankings of the football team at Florida State University, where Joiner is a tenured professor, and Ohio State University, which is a perennial football powerhouse. When the team was highly ranked, the suicide rate in the two cities—Gainesville and Columbus, respectively—was lower, Joiner found.[6]

Other studies support this. In one study of 30 metropolitan areas in the U.S. over 20 years, researchers noted that the suicide rate went down when the area’s pro team made the playoffs and went on to win a champion­ship.[7] Conversely, the defeat of a high-profile soccer team in England led to increased cases of self-poisoning, according to a different study.[8] In a third study, suicides of young men increased in Quebec when the Montreal Canadiens hockey team lost an early-round playoff series.[9]

People joke about “living and dying” with their favorite team, but the sense of belongingness that someone feels rooting for a team can be undone when that team loses and its season is over. It’s easy to say that no one should take sports so seriously, but as a fan myself, I’m aware of the lure.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Art of Asking Questions
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

The Art of Asking Questions

Being interested is at the heart of genuine connection.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Being invited to share signals care; assuming others will volunteer can leave them feeling unseen.
  • Sharing a similar experience can build connection—or hijack the conversation.
  • Good follow-up questions grow from listening, not from planning what you’ll say next.
Me, me, me, me, me. Now, what do you think about me?
Source: Public Domain Pictures

I recently got invited to a Halloween party where I knew only the hosts. People close to me think I am a major extrovert, so they may assume that going to a party filled with strangers would be easy-peasy for me.

But the truth is, I had to force myself to go. Quite honestly, I love deep, meaningful, one-on-one conversations—the deeper, the better—but small talk with new people? That’s a completely different story.

I decided to push myself outside my comfort zone to not only go to this party, but show up in a 1920s flapper costume. I definitely got an A+ for effort.

Although I had a good time, I must admit that, in some ways, the evening left me feeling empty.

Why?

Have you ever left a conversation knowing practically everything about another person’s life, only to realize that they learned almost nothing about yours?

They told you about their children, their travels, their work, their recent challenges. You listened. You asked questions. And you waited for a little curiosity to come your way.

But it never did.

Or perhaps they asked a question, but your answer merely provided a launching pad for another story about themselves.

“You’re a therapist?” “Yes,” I respond. And then I hear, “I once went to a therapist. I can’t believe what happened to me...”

What about, “What kind of therapy do you do?” or “What’s it like to work with couples teetering on divorce?” or "What do you do for fun when you're not working?"

Sharing Experiences Versus Taking Over a Conversation

When people share their own experiences, it can be a way of connecting. But there is a difference between offering something that deepens a conversation and taking it over.

As a therapist, I have spent nearly five decades asking questions. Yet you don’t need professional training to say, “What was that like for you?” or “Tell me more about that,” or “What happened next?”

Whatever happened to curiosity? Or giving people enough time to share their experiences without interruption?

Why is that so difficult?

Some people derive pleasure from talking about themselves. They like to entertain or impress. Others assume that if you have something to share, you will volunteer it.

But what they don’t realize is that being invited matters. It shows interest and caring.

And sometimes, we are simply so busy thinking about what we want to say next that we aren’t listening carefully enough to notice the opportunities to connect on a deeper level.

I don’t necessarily believe that people who dominate conversations are uncaring. In fact, I often assume that people who don’t ask questions probably grew up in homes where few meaningful questions were asked of them.

But regardless of the reasons that people prefer talking about themselves in conversation with you, there is loneliness in feeling unseen.

How to Ask Follow-Up Questions Without Interrogating

The art of asking questions begins with listening to the answer—and allowing it to influence what you ask next.

If a friend says that she is low on energy these days, instead of saying, “Yeah, me too,” we might ask if something unusual is going on in her life, if she has been taking good care of herself physically and emotionally, or what thoughts she has about why she feels depleted.

We don’t have to interrogate people. We can follow what they seem eager to share, respect what they prefer to keep private, and offer our own thoughts along the way. The goal is a genuine exchange, not a cross-examination.

Try noticing your next conversation. When someone finishes speaking, do you think about what you might ask to deepen your understanding of the speaker’s experience? Or do you find yourself immediately thinking how their story relates to you?

Do an experiment. Before you shift the conversation away from the speaker, consider asking one more question.

Being interesting has its place. So does being interested.

Too often, we underestimate how much the latter matters.

So, what do you think of my thoughts today? Inquiring minds want to know.

item.title: Why Our Country Needs More School Psychologists
item.description:
Psych Careers

Why Our Country Needs More School Psychologists

School psychologists are agents for positive change, but there aren’t enough.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • There is a national shortage of school psychologists.
  • The role of school psychologists is misunderstood or unknown to many laypeople.
  • School psychologists are trained to respond to the range of problems that children face at schools.

Imagine it’s your first day of second grade. You’re feeling a mix of excitement and nervousness as you walk to your classroom. You walk into the wrong one and are greeted with stares from third graders. You quickly turn around and leave the room when you accidentally bump into someone. You look up, and a smiling face greets you, radiating immense warmth, and asks if you’re lost. You nod your head, and tears begin to well in your eyes. This person reassures you and asks you to take a deep “whale breath” before walking you to your classroom and then gives you a high five.

The School Psychologist Shortage

That person is a school psychologist, and our country needs more of them. In November, the National Association of School Psychologists (NASP) celebrates National School Psychology Week, which recognizes the essential roles they have within schools and communities. The role of school psychologists is so essential that NASP, the American Psychological Association (APA), and even former President Joe Biden have all called attention to the shortage of school psychologists in this country. Experts recommend that schools have one school psychologist for every 500 children, yet the national average is more than 1,000 students to one school psychologist. Despite all this, the profession of school psychology continues to be diminished by other branches of psychology, as well as misunderstood or unknown to lay people.

Think of a school psychologist as a special education teacher, administrator, counselor, and advocate all in one. School psychologists administer psychological assessments; facilitate individual and group counseling; perform interventions; participate in collaborations between schools, communities, and families; engage in consultation; advocate for systems-level changes; and more. School psychologists are known to “wear different hats” due to the broad range of skills that they employ on any given work day. Their strengths and talents know no bounds.

School Psychology’s Origins

The official practice of school psychology emerged in 1896 when Lightner Witmer opened the first psychology clinic at the University of Pennsylvania. Witmer, considered the founder of both clinical and school psychology, created this clinic to develop remediation plans for children presenting with learning, attention, and behavioral problems in school. Many of the children assessed in his clinic met criteria for what is now understood as dyslexia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability. The children assessed in his clinic were referred to by teachers, parents, and other school-based professionals.

In his clinic, Witmer and his multidisciplinary team of physicians, social workers, and other professionals worked to diagnose children’s presenting problems through the “clinical method.” This method involved a referral system, testing, review of records, and treatment, which more closely resembled “modern school psychology than it would be to today’s practice of clinical psychology.” Witmer even discreetly implied that the “clinical psychologist” was in fact a “school psychologist,” thus prompting the graduate level of instruction in psychology to be tailored to school teachers and psychologists who work in the schools.

The most important work of this lifetime is raising, educating, and supporting our country’s children, and school psychologists are fully capable of meeting their academic, developmental, behavioral, and psychological needs. Moreover, as schools continue to be unfortunate sites of shootings, bullying and harassment, and in rare instances, suicides, school psychologists remain uniquely capable of responding to these crises and emergencies. They are specifically trained on how to handle crises in uncertain situations, conduct threat assessments, and de-escalate situations. However, even with the abundance of training that they have, school psychologists endure the misperception that their training is somehow less rigorous than that of their colleagues in clinical or counseling psychology.

School psychology students are less likely to secure APA-accredited doctoral internships, which, in part, is attributed to internship directors’ unwillingness to review applications from school psychology students. One potential reason for this unwillingness is the misperception that school psychology students lack preparation in counseling and mental health interventions. This is surprising, considering that the curriculum in clinical, counseling, and school psychology is more similar than it is different.

Furthermore, school psychology graduate students are not only trained to understand school systems and special education law, but they also gain knowledge in clinical and counseling psychology. School psychology graduate students learn about developmental psychopathology, mental disorders, counseling theories, and therapeutic interventions, which form a solid foundation in understanding human functioning.

For quite some time, schools, particularly those in rural areas, have grown accustomed to supporting the needs of students without school psychologists. This is risky territory given how high the stakes are. So how could this issue be solved? For now, the best approach is to encourage prospective applicants to clinical and counseling programs to apply to school psychology programs. If a qualified applicant is interested in working with children, supporting children’s social and emotional learning, being an advocate, and working with families, you are urged to consider this field!

item.title: Why Your Wife Doesn’t Want Sex (and What Actually Helps)
item.description:
Sex

Why Your Wife Doesn’t Want Sex (and What Actually Helps)

Understanding responsive desire can help you stop taking “no” personally.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Desire differences are one of the most common problems couples discuss in therapy.
  • Most men experience spontaneous desire. Most women need to be turned on before they want sex.
  • Pressure and stress shut down responsive desire, so pushing harder usually backfires.

Arms crossed, jaw tight, eyes on the floor. As a couples therapist, I see this man in my office all the time. He says, “I’m tired of being the only one who wants it.” When you’ve been turned down over and over, it starts to feel less like what you’re hearing is “not tonight,” and more like it’s “not you.”

Maybe you feel like you have tried everything to make your partner want sex with you. It just seems like she never does, no matter what you do. Beyond feeling sexually frustrated, you feel rejected, unwanted, and unattractive. You may tell yourself stories that something is wrong with you, like your sexual performance or the way you look, or stories about how your wife is the problem, such as that she has a “low libido” and needs to work on her desire herself.

These stories make sense. They’re also usually wrong.

Desire discrepancies are common. Far from being the exception, differences in sexual desire are a part of most relationships (Fogel Mersy & Vencill, 2023). Your relationship is probably normal. And so is your wife.

The Science: When Arousal Comes First, Before Desire

Your wife not wanting sex out of the blue is not the same as your wife not wanting sex with you. She probably does experience sexual desire, just not in the way that you expect.

Most men (75%) have a primarily “spontaneous” desire style; the feeling of randomly, out of the blue, wanting sex. However, for most women, sexual arousal actually precedes the feeling of sexual desire. Only 15% of women experience primarily spontaneous desire; the other 85% of women experience “responsive desire,” meaning sexual desire that occurs in response to sexual arousal or sexual stimuli. Let me say that again: for women, most often, physiological arousal comes first, and sexual desire comes after.

In my opinion, this is far and away the most common misconception about sex there is. Blame it on the patriarchy: because most of our ideas about sexuality are based on the “male as default,” most people in our society expect women’s sexual desire to be just like the average man’s. If spontaneous desire is the only kind you’ve ever experienced, it’s easy to assume it’s the only kind.

What you can do is create the conditions where her desire has room to show up. You can help her want sex by doing a few things: (1) help reduce her stress and fatigue, (2) build arousal for her pleasure, (3) cut the pressure.

Working With Your Wife’s Nervous System

Your wife, just like you, has two competing parts of her nervous system: the parasympathetic “rest-and-digest” branch and the sympathetic “fight-or-flight” branch. It’s hard for your wife to want to have sex when her body feels that a predator is chasing her. And more often than not, the stimuli that are activating her threat response are not actual predators. They are the mental load, unequal household and childcare work, body image, worry about whether her desire is “normal,” and feeling like sex is a debt she owes. It’s hard to feel sexy while mentally running the grocery list, the pediatrician appointment, and tomorrow’s carpool.

Why Pushing Makes It Worse

I see a self-reinforcing cycle in my couple clients. Stress reduces desire, and reduced desire creates more stress, which further reduces desire.

And your wife’s worry about letting you down becomes another thing that shuts down her desire.

You initiate, and she says, “Not tonight.” You feel rejected and either push harder or withdraw into sulking and resentment. Your wife feels pressure or guilt, her stress rises, and desire drops further. You feel more rejected. You’re doing what makes sense. It just doesn’t work.

You may have noticed that your wife starts to turn down not just sex, but non-sexual physical touch as well. When she associates every touch with pressure for sex, her body learns to brace against touch. And you end up feeling even more unwanted and far away.

The chasing dynamic (Nagoski, 2015) is the enemy, not your partner, not you.

What Actually Helps

  • Affection with no destination. To break out of the chasing cycle, touch needs to be uncoupled from pressure for sex. You need to touch, hug, kiss, and seek closeness with your wife without the expectation that it will lead to sex. Paradoxically, you’ll likely have more sex when you stop pushing for it. And make it ok for your wife to say no. No sulking, guilt-tripping, or expressing anger when she turns you down. The safer it is for her to say no, the easier it becomes for her to say yes.

  • Build arousal for her pleasure, not as a route to yes. The goal should be connection and mutual enjoyment. Sex is a possible outcome of touch, but it needs to be far from the target. Ask her what makes her feel cared for and loved, and do those things. Safety is the baseline for responsive desire. Get curious about what kinds of touch or words turn her on and activate her desire.

  • Lighten her load, but not as a trade. There’s a reason couples who share household chores more fairly have sex more often than couples where she carries most of the load (Carlson et al., 2016). And it’s not because she’s punishing you for leaving dishes in the sink or rewarding you for vacuuming. It’s because when she doesn’t have to carry stress alone, she moves out of fight-or-flight and into a nervous system state where her body is more likely to feel desire.

One important caveat here: if you clean the house so you’ll get sex, she will feel it, and it will just add more pressure. Show her that this is about her well-being, not yours.

Understanding Desire Styles Changes Your Sex Life

When I explain responsive desire to husbands, their shoulders drop, and their jaws loosen. They start to understand that there is hope for a better sex life. There’s nothing wrong with you, your wife, or your marriage.

Work with your wife’s nervous system to help her responsive desire come online. Help lower her stress by taking things off her plate, like the laundry. Help her feel safe by removing the pressure. When safety is mixed with physiological arousal, desire has room to show up. The fastest way to her desire turns out to be the long way around.

item.title: Why Cognitive Surrender Feels Alright
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why Cognitive Surrender Feels Alright

Some of our basic tendencies make it easy to hand over critical thinking to AI.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • “Cognitive surrender” involves handing over critical thinking or judgment to AI instead of doing it yourself.
  • A need for closure, a desire not to think hard, and AI's confident tone can make it easy to accept AI answers.
  • To avoid cognitive surrender to AI, one should interrogate its answers and keep doing hard mental work.

Imagine your boss asks you to analyze some data and then write up a report on it. You are already busy with several projects and approaching deadlines for other reports, so you generate a draft of the report using an AI tool. The report looks polished, tells a coherent and sensible story about the data, and includes statistics to back up its points.

Do you check for typos, then turn it in? Or do you read it carefully and check it against your own analysis of the data?

The first choice would be considered “cognitive surrender.”

Cognitive surrender means handing over critical thinking or judgment to an AI tool instead of doing it yourself. It is moving from using AI to augment your thinking to using it to do your thinking.

This can lead to serious problems, including becoming worse at critical thinking. When you offload critical thinking to technology, your ability to do that kind of thinking can erode, because the skills of thinking aren’t practiced. Of course, another problem with cognitive surrender is that AI can be wrong. When you do it on something important (e.g., a class grade, a major project at work, a big financial decision), there could be terrible consequences.

Considering those possible consequences of cognitive surrender, why would anyone do it? There are several psychological phenomena that might make it quite easy to surrender even if you don’t intend to. Here are three:

  1. Need for cognitive closure. Some people are highly motivated to find a coherent story, to put pieces together and reduce ambiguity. This is called the need for cognitive closure. A tool that can do the hard work of gathering and sorting disparate information, and then give you a crisp, sensible summary, would be very attractive to use if you have a high need for closure. Such a tool would reduce ambiguity much faster than thinking through and analyzing a lot of information on your own.
  2. Confidence as cue. A message that is delivered with confidence and certainty is more likely to be accepted. Conversational AI tools have been trained to use a certain, confident tone. Even without consciously considering it, that tone can make an AI’s output easier to see as accurate and correct.
  3. Thinking hard is hard. People often find that thinking through a difficult problem is simply not pleasant. Even for those people who like to think deeply, sometimes things are just too busy to stop and spend the necessary time to think through a difficult issue. AI can so easily step in and handle it for you. Why not let it? That convenient relief of a burdensome task can be hard to forgo.

Apply the Science to Using AI

These research findings, however, could also point us towards strategies for using AI more safely and effectively.

First, don’t seize on the first answer AI gives you. Interrogate the tool, ask it to argue another perspective, or ask it to give sources that support its conclusions, and go and read them. One important thing to remember is that most AIs are trained to deliver what users most like, not necessarily what’s most accurate. So, resist the temptation to accept the first answer.

Second, think of an AI answer as a sales pitch. During development, AI models are generally rewarded for being confident. Just like you might discount a salesperson’s confidence about their product, you may want to discount an AI’s confidence in its conclusions and answers.

And third, if you want your critical thinking skills to stay sharp, you probably need to practice them. If you find yourself outsourcing a lot of hard mental work to AI tools, you could hold back and go through the difficult slog on some of that work. Just like working hard physically makes your body healthier, working hard mentally may keep your brain healthier.

Some of these strategies can be done with a few extra prompts. Because AI tools are so good at following instructions, you can instruct them to help you avoid cognitive surrender if you want to.

Uncritically accepting AI output can be helpful at times, especially when you have crafted appropriate prompts, built a custom agent, or otherwise analyzed how the tool will handle its assignment. But the costs of this surrender could sometimes outweigh the convenience and productivity boost.
