item.title: When Someone You Love Suddenly Feels Like the Enemy
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder

When Someone You Love Suddenly Feels Like the Enemy

How all-or-nothing thinking can derail relationships for people with BPD.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • In BPD, splitting can cause sudden shifts in how we perceive the people closest to us.
  • One hurtful interaction can temporarily overshadow everything positive about a relationship.
  • Taking a broader perspective can help us respond to conflict without damaging important relationships.

Imagine you're telling your partner about a frustrating phone call you had with your mom, and they jokingly remark, "Well, we all know how much you love being right."

You know they're teasing, but you feel yourself starting to get angry. In fact, without meaning to, you’re now thinking of the last time your partner made an off-color comment. And the time before that. Before you know it, you’ve written them off as insensitive and uncaring. Despite starting the evening looking forward to hanging out together, you’re now questioning whether you even want to be with this person.

Yes, your partner's comment was insensitive, and it's certainly reasonable to feel hurt. At the same time, in the heat of the moment, that single interaction has overshadowed all the positive experiences you've shared and the qualities you usually appreciate about your partner.

All-or-Nothing Thinking in Relationships

For people with borderline personality disorder (BPD), experiences like this are really common. In fact, alternating between idealizing and devaluing others is one of the diagnostic criteria for this condition. When things are going smoothly, a partner, friend, or family member might seem like the most loving, supportive person in the world. However, that same person may suddenly seem selfish or untrustworthy after a disappointing interaction.

This pattern is sometimes called splitting, a form of black-and-white thinking in which people have difficulty holding positive and negative qualities in mind at the same time. Rather than recognizing that someone can be a caring partner who occasionally says something insensitive, the negative experience overshadows everything else.

These sudden shifts in how we perceive the people closest to us can be disorienting, making it difficult to maintain stable, lasting relationships. Indeed, negative perceptions of others, however temporary, can lead to behaviors that cause lasting consequences. For example, if you're convinced your partner doesn't care about you, you might lash out, accuse them of being selfish, or threaten to end the relationship. Alternatively, you might withdraw, stop responding to messages, or push them away before they have the chance to reject you.

Finding the Gray in Your Relationships

In BPD Compass, an evidence-based treatment for BPD, there are two strategies that are particularly relevant for combating the difficulties all-or-nothing thinking can cause.

The first is the Relationship Compass, a tool for deciding your goals for a given relationship. The Relationship Compass replaces the cardinal directions (North, South, East, and West) with relationship objectives: I Need something; I want to Set a limit; I Want to get closer; I’m considering Ending a relationship.

The Relationship Compass helps you identify what you ultimately want from a relationship before you're in the middle of an upsetting interaction. That way, when your emotions threaten to take the wheel, you’ll have already planned behaviors that align with your compass.

Another important strategy from BPD Compass is the Dimensions of Trust exercise. Here, you’re asked to consider the various ways you can trust the specific people in your life. The dimensions on which other people are rated (0 to 100 percent) include the degree to which someone is on time, emotionally supportive, does what they say they’re going to do, keeps your confidences, is trusted to watch your kids, etc.

Not only do you get to see that most people fall somewhere between 0 and 100 percent on any given dimension, but you also begin to recognize that someone can be highly trustworthy in some areas and less so in others. The next time you're tempted to write someone off as completely untrustworthy, you can revisit these ratings to remind yourself of the bigger picture and decide how to respond based on their actual strengths and limitations.

Together, these strategies create some distance between how we feel about someone in a particular moment and how we choose to respond. We can acknowledge that someone has hurt us without losing sight of everything else we know about them or the relationship.

Seeing the Whole Person

No matter how solid a relationship may be, there will be times when you hurt each other's feelings. It is important to recognize those shortcomings without allowing them to erase everything else we know about that person.

For people with BPD, this can take practice. Over time, you can get better at seeing your relationships in shades of gray; in other words, it is possible to see both the positive and negative qualities of someone at the same time. As you strengthen this ability, you’ll also get better at choosing reactions that align with what you ultimately want, rather than how you feel in a particular moment.

item.title: How to Know You're Going Through 'Couple Burnout'
item.description:
Burnout

How to Know You're Going Through 'Couple Burnout'

Stress and exhaustion can pass between partners—not just stay with one person.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Burnout can spill between work and relationships, compounding exhaustion in both.
  • One partner’s burnout can increase the other’s, making it a shared challenge.
  • Open communication and mutual support help couples address burnout as a team.
Source: Kenneth Surillo / Pexels

A research paper published in Social Psychology Quarterly introduces a 10-item scale that measures “burnout” within couples, providing mental health experts and the public with a tool that can help couples address feelings of exhaustion and indifference within their relationships.

According to the researchers, burnout refers to feelings of mental, physical, and emotional exhaustion that lead to feelings of disengagement and a lowered sense of accomplishment. It is often the result of over-involvement in emotionally demanding responsibilities.

Although burnout is commonly understood as a work-related experience, studies show that burnout can occur within romantic relationships, too. The exhaustion we’re used to feeling after a long and stressful day of work can also be felt when we disconnect or detach from our partner. Even more concerning, these two types of burnout can interact with one another in detrimental ways.

'Burnout Contagion' Can Infect All Aspects Of Your Life

In the study, the authors explain that the experience of burnout in one area of life can spill over into others. In essence, if you’re experiencing stress or strain in your relationship, there is a decent chance that you’ll experience burnout in your work life, too.

Moreover, the researchers also found that one partner’s experience of burnout can cross over to the other partner. Essentially, if one partner expresses stress with their work or in the relationship, the other partner’s experience of burnout may also increase.

These findings highlight how burnout isn’t just a one-dimensional issue; it’s a contagion that can spread between different aspects of one’s life. If you’re feeling overwhelmed or strained in your relationship, it’s likely to spill into your work life, and vice versa.

When we’re burning the candle at both ends, our well-being suffers. And perhaps the most eye-opening discovery is that burnout isn’t just an individual struggle—it’s a shared experience in couples.

Couple’s Burnout Measure

To measure the experience of burnout in couples, the researchers developed a 10-item scale that captures symptoms of emotional, mental, and physical exhaustion in a romantic partnership.

The test, intended to be answered on a scale from “never” to “always,” is as follows:

When you think about your marriage or intimate relationship overall, how often have you felt:

  1. Tired
  2. Disappointed with your spouse or intimate partner
  3. Hopeless
  4. Trapped
  5. Helpless
  6. Depressed
  7. Weak or sickly
  8. Insecure or like a failure
  9. Difficulties sleeping
  10. “I’ve had it”

If you frequently grapple with these 10 feelings, you might be experiencing couple’s burnout. The best thing you can do in this situation is to reach out to your partner and let them in on your feelings and experiences.

Remember, you’re not alone. Burnout often infiltrates the relationship space like an uninvited guest. By actively supporting one another, communicating openly, and making a conscious effort to re-center yourselves, you’re not just tackling burnout as individuals; you’re navigating it as a team.

The significance of supporting each other when one or both partners are experiencing burnout cannot be overstated. It’s like holding an umbrella together in a rainstorm—you shield each other from the downpour. Finding that balance, both in the hustle of your careers and the intimacy of your romantic life, isn’t just an option, but a lifeline. It’s the key to surviving and thriving in your relationship.

item.title: Work Couples Therapy
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Work Couples Therapy

Work couples can benefit from couples therapy too.

Posted November 9, 2026

What exactly is a couple? The most popular answer would be: two people involved in a romantic relationship. However, that “romantic” label eliminates many non-romantic couples who are also in relationships. It’s normal to assume that couples therapy is only for romantic couples, but there are others who might also benefit from the experience. These people can be coworkers, cofounders, writing teams, bandmates, best friends, sisters, brothers, roommates, and other people involved in relationships who, while not the traditional client base for couples therapy, can also be in need of and benefit from the work and approach of traditional couples therapy.

My practice includes couples therapy with work couples. This started with my work with writing teams, which started with my experience as a working screenwriter working alongside writing teams. I never developed a writing partnership on my own when I was a screenwriter, but the experience of working with writing teams as a writer naturally led me to work with writing teams as a therapist. Now this part of my practice has expanded to include business partners and co-founders in different industries. Sometimes these couples have deep roots of friendship, often including the experience of growing up together, going to college together, or some other kind of background that preceded their business partnership.

What’s the point of couples therapy? To learn how to experience more happiness in our relationships. Which sounds like it would be great for all kinds of couples, not just romantic ones. Of course, one aspect of romantic relationships that many romantic couples see as representative of the state of their relationship, and a battleground for their issues of conflict and communication, is sex. That’s not to say resolving issues related to sex is the key to couples therapy, but that this is an issue our work couples do not have to deal with (or they do, in which case they just crossed the line into traditional romantic couples therapy).

I see both romantic couples and work couples, and much of the work is similar, but the main difference is that work couples don’t share a bedroom (or do all the stuff that romantic couples do in the bedroom). This means that romantic couples often experience a greater amount of intimacy than work couples, but that doesn’t mean that work couples don’t have intimate relationships. They do. And one of the ways I work with work couples is by increasing their experience of intimacy with each other.

Intimacy means different things to different people. For many people intimacy means being physically intimate. However, physical closeness (sex) is not intimacy. Physical closeness (sex) can, however, help create intimacy, which is traditionally defined as feelings of closeness fostered by emotional connection and support. Sex can make us feel incredibly intimate with our partner, but there are other ways of increasing intimacy between partners besides sex. Like what, you ask? Like the following: Being honest about feelings. Sharing emotional history. Talking about hopes and fears. In short, being vulnerable. It is this kind of vulnerability that is the hallmark of increased intimacy and happier relationships, and something we strive for in romantic couples therapy, but something we don’t always consider when thinking about ways to improve our work relationships.

Here’s how that might work: A work couple might come to me with issues related to frustration with each other’s behavior. This behavior might be affecting their work in a negative way, and be worth resolving in order for their business to succeed in the way they want it to. They will often come into therapy with complaints about each other, and conversely with justifications for why they act they way they do, and cause their partner to complain about them.

The work here for me is not so much to pass judgment on who is right and who is wrong and what the right way to proceed is. It is more about getting curious about each partner’s behavior and the reasons for it. I’m not some business guru who can get two co-founders on the same page by creating a relationship business plan for them to follow. I’m a therapist who wants to know why one partner’s behavior seems to trigger the other partner, leading to conflict that makes it difficult for them to support each other.

This usually entails moving away from the interpersonal communication issues and digging more deeply into the emotional history of each partner. Sometimes there’s pushback on this. “Why are we talking about my childhood? Who cares what my mom’s mom was like? What does my parents’ divorce have to do with the business?” The reason we get into this kind of deep dive is because we want to learn where each partner learned to act the way they do in their current relationship. One partner’s frustration with the other’s aversion to risk taking might be lessened by learning that their partner’s father was an alcoholic gambler who lost their savings and put their future in jeopardy.

Through this act of sharing intimate details about childhood and parental relationships we might move from a frustrated “I don’t get why my partner can’t do X or keeps avoiding Y” and toward a more supportive understanding of “I get why this issue triggers my partner and how I can change my behavior to help them." It is this kind of intimacy and understanding that strengthens relationships, and which is often harder to achieve in work relationships. The bedroom setting of romantic relationships, the opportunity for pillow talk, the way physical intimacy (sex) can lead directly to emotional intimacy—these all present opportunities for romantic couples to create the intimacy and understanding that strengthens relationships in ways that are not available to work couples.

Thank goodness for practitioners of work couples therapy, I say, as it provides a place for all couples, regardless of romantic status, a place to work toward happier relationships.

item.title: The Journey to Reconnect With the Self
item.description:
Rejection Sensitivity

The Journey to Reconnect With the Self

Moving beyond rejection sensitive dysphoria.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Rejection sensitive dysphoria often causes us to disconnect from the self.
  • To restore self connection, we can begin to connect to our interests and engage in creativity.
  • Reflecting on our values and practicing self-love as an action can also fortify our sense of self.

How can you reconnect with yourself if you have rejection sensitive dysphoria? Many of us with this lose touch with ourselves, as rejection sensitive dysphoria is an intense emotional sensitivity to being judged, criticized, or failing at essential roles or relationships. To avoid the intense pain of rejection, many people who experience this dysphoria develop habits like perfectionism, people-pleasing, and masking. These behavioral patterns make rejection sensitive dysphoria more than just how we interact with rejection; they can activate these patterns and significantly affect our lives (Mutti-Driscoll, 2026).

Tapping Into 'Wise Mind' and Authentic Self

To help reverse the effects, reconnecting with yourself is important.

To do that, it helps to use the "wise mind" concept from Marsha Linehan's dialectical behavior therapy. According to Linehan, we all have a wise mind: the part of ourselves not driven solely by logic or emotion, but a hybrid of the two. This is our most mature self, and even if we cannot access this mind, it is still there.

Richard Schwartz, who created internal family systems theory, also examined this: beyond our reactive patterns of avoidance and control, there is self. This is our true self or our most authentic self—grounded, embodied, authentic, and never lost. Even if we feel mired in attempts to avoid or control, it is still there, and we can still find it. That is the part of the journey where we can reconnect with who we really are (Dore, 2021).

Four Ways to Reconnect

Reconnecting with yourself is a journey. I wish I could say it happens instantaneously, but it is a journey. And these are things we will have to do over time to establish and maintain that connection.

1. Think about ourselves as children

We can have compassion and advocate for that child. The reason we might advocate for ourselves as children is that it can be easier to have compassion for our younger selves. Also, experts think there was something pure about us, especially before age 10, before we started absorbing expectations. If we can access what we liked to do and enjoyed, we can sometimes reconnect with something more authentic than how we became as we advanced through the teen and adult years.

2. Engage in creativity

Oftentimes, that is a strength for neurodivergent people—getting back to creativity if we have strayed from it. We can reflect on past creative moments, not just when we are making art; we can be creative in problem-solving, helping others, or organizing people. We can intentionally tap into current interests we may have felt embarrassed about and have not pursued, or we can reignite old ones.

3. Clarify what is important

Think about what is important to us, and try to reconnect with the actions that bring us closer to it and those that take us further away. Developing this is like a foundation for our true self. When we know what is important to us, it's easier to access that self. We can find ways to remember it and clarify what that means, making it less abstract: What would it mean to live my values each day?

Values are important; it is not just feel-good fluff. For many of us with ADHD and autism, connecting to what is meaningful is huge for stimulating our brains and motivating us to persist and get things done (Solden and Frank, 2019).

4. Practice self-love as an action

Even if we do not feel super loving toward ourselves, we can still take actions that care for ourselves (Dore, 2021). We can be the parent who takes care of us: What would we do for ourselves even if it was hard to initiate or too boring? What would we do to show ourselves love? We can also make those tasks less painful and more engaging through rewards and accountability.

Progress, Not Perfection

You can choose your own adventure when you reconnect.

A reminder: This is a journey. If you try one of these strategies and it doesn't work instantaneously, it is not a failure, and you are not a failure. It is a journey, and putting it in an all-or-nothing box is not the goal:

  • I am either successful or not
  • I am either healed or broken
  • I am either there or not there

The journey of personal growth is up and down. It is not about arriving, which I know we'd prefer. It is about holding these opposites at the same time: We can make progress, knowing there is more to do. That is okay. We can still celebrate our growth and be proud of ourselves while knowing we still want to improve—that is part of being human.

Any small action we can take to reconnect with ourselves is an important investment in healing from rejection sensitive dysphoria. I hope you will join me in this important journey! You are worth it.

item.title: Breaking Down Political Boundaries
item.description:
Politics

Breaking Down Political Boundaries

How values shape our views.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • We all hold similar core values, but each of us ranks them in a different order.
  • Create a dialogue by asking others what they value most to help you find common ground.
  • Find one value you share and use it as an anchor point in your discussions.

After many surprising elections these past few months, many are bewildered that people's values could seemingly shift so easily. However, our moral values—what we believe is right and wrong—aren’t random and rarely change. They’re shaped by experience, genetics, and upbringing.

Our common values

According to moral foundations theory, most people's values fall into six key categories:

  • Care: We dislike seeing suffering in others, and want to help.
  • Fairness: We expect to be treated as we treat others.
  • Loyalty: We put trust in those close to us.
  • Authority: We respect and even admire strong, legitimate leaders.
  • Sanctity/Purity: We avoid things that disgust us.
  • Liberty: We own our lives and our choices.

Most people care about all of these. We just rank them differently. Researchers found that libertarians rank liberty highest, liberals rank care and fairness highest, and conservatives rank all six about equally.

When we assume others don’t value what we do, we miss the point. Often, they simply prioritize different moral foundations. Instead we could be asking: What do they value most?

Find the doorway instead of hitting the wall

You are unlikely to shift people's political positions, but you can still find ways to see eye-to-eye.

Look for one value you both rank high. A shared value works like a doorway. Arguing builds a wall.

Begin by demonstrating a true curiosity, a chance to learn. Swap questions like “Why do you think that?”—which sounds like a challenge—for “Oh, interesting. So would you say...?” This helps establish you as someone who is interested and trying to understand rather than someone who is trying to win an argument.

Source: Anett Szekeres/Pexels

Once you have an understanding of their point of view, name a value you share. Say you rank care first and your uncle ranks liberty first. You both want people to thrive. He believes they thrive when they are free to choose. You believe they thrive when someone looks out for them. Same goal, different road. Start there.

This is also an anchor point. If the conversation starts feeling like a debate, you can always fall back to this: "Hey, we are all here to make sure people are able to do what they want in life."

Be someone’s exception

After you build a connection, keep it alive. Become a person they feel safe talking to, the exception in their life. Maybe they say, “Oh, not all liberals are like that.” Maybe you hear, “Not all conservatives are like that.” Either way, you have opened a door rather than built a wall.

If each of us becomes another person’s exception, we can keep our conversations constructive.

Pick one person this week. Ask what matters most to them.

item.title: Perfectionism Isn’t the Problem
item.description:
Perfectionism

Perfectionism Isn’t the Problem

How we can support adolescents to examine the pressure to be perfect.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Internal and external pressures drive perfectionism
  • Adolescents are under pressure to be academically, socially and aesthetically perfect
  • We can help adolescents to make sense of what perfectionism means to them
Who decides what perfect really means?
Source: Pixabay/Alexas_Fotos

I speak to many adolescents and young adults who call themselves “perfectionists”. Often, their parents, if they are involved in the referral, want me to get them to change—by which they mean, lower their standards. Or at least lower their standards in some domains, the ones that parents perceive as less important, such as appearance, friendship, dating, Snapchat streaks and TikTok reels. As a psychotherapist, it’s not my job to “fix” behaviour or “correct” thought patterns, but it is my job to try to make sense of it. As something of a perfectionist myself, I don’t see aiming high as problematic and I admire young people with ambition, who strive to be their best selves. What I do see as a problem, however, is the pressure to be perfect. When the pressure is internal, it can be debilitating and counterproductive. When it comes from external influences it often feels contrary – “Aim high, anything less than the best is less than good enough, but also; stop being such a perfectionist!”

Young people in contemporary society are under more pressure than ever before, and the bar keeps getting higher. In the UK, GCSEs are graded 1–9, where a 7 is roughly equivalent to the old A grade, an 8 is an A* and a 9 is even higher than that.

An “A” isn’t enough at A* level either, since the introduction of A*. So, being an A-grade student means you’re less than perfect, and that’s perceived as less than good enough.

Most young people are now expected to apply to university, rather than an elite minority—even those who struggle academically, setting them up for more pressure and more experiences of being less than perfect. They’re under pressure to know what comes next and have their sights set on a “good career”, even though jobs are scarcer, because there’s so much competition, because there are so many more graduates. Meanwhile, the social pressure to be perfect involves an impossible checklist. Girls have to be slim and curvy and beautiful with perfectly aligned teeth and brows and lashes and not look like they tried. Boys have to be buff. All genders have to be partnered up and smashing their “relationship goals”. They need to be popular and having so much fun all the time, while their imperfect brains and their imperfect bodies are still developing.

Adolescents tend also to be more susceptible than most to the modern affliction of “compare and despair”, comparing their worst feeling self on their worst performing day to someone else’s carefully curated, filtered, photo-shopped, perfect self on Instagram. On Instagram, everyone looks as if they’re living their best life. They don’t share the cramming-for-exams all-nighters and their less-than-perfect grades; they share the all-night parties, where everyone looks super-glam, which you scroll through at home feeling super-glum. They don’t share the misery of dating fatigue, relationship heartbreak, friendship fallings-out or family conflict; they share picture-perfect group shots in glamorous locations—also curated, also filtered. They don’t share sh*t days at work or sh*t days at uni, or sh*t days at school; they show the fabulous fun they’re having at freshers’ week or away days—all carefully curated and filtered.

So, when I meet an adolescent perfectionist, I don’t tell them to lower their standards; I tell them it’s great that they have standards. I don’t suggest they stop comparing themselves with other people; I assure them that’s human nature. But I do wonder where the pressure to be perfect is coming from and where it’s landing: Is it internal or external? Does it apply to some areas more than others? And I explore whether that internal and external messaging aligns with their own attitudes and beliefs. I’m curious about how they measure perfectionism too—by whose standards, and whether those standards are realistic and align with their own. Ultimately, I help adolescents make sense of what perfectionism means to them, so they can be their own version of “best self” and curate their own “best life” and be content with their own version of perfect.

item.title: 11 Tools to Deal With Your Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

11 Tools to Deal With Your Anxiety

Treatment of anxiety often improves medical symptoms.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety is a feeling of worry that can cause development of physical and/or psychological pressure.
  • Anxiety in small doses can be a good thing, as it can help you act more deliberately and carefully.
  • One of the most effective tools against anxiety is changing your sensory input.
Source: Mishchenko Svitlana/Shutterstock

Anxiety can be both a symptom and a cause of medical issues. For example, I treat a lot of patients who live with breathing disorders. Struggling to breathe is hard enough to manage, but anxiety can make it worse.

I also meet many people who are dealing with physical symptoms like stomach pain, headaches, and fainting—and when we get to the bottom of their problems, we often find anxiety at the root.

So, what is it? Anxiety is a feeling of worry or nervousness that you can experience as physical pressure, psychological pressure, or both.

It can be a minor inconvenience—like a nagging sense of being on edge—or it can be an overwhelming feeling that demands all your attention.

At times, it can even get in the way of your power to think logically. For example, a student might feel so much anxiety about taking a test that they skip class and miss the test altogether. The result of that choice might be getting a zero—which is definitely worse than whatever grade they might have received if they would have shown up.

In this post, we will review 11 tools you can use to deal better with anxiety.

1. Take a Pause

If you feel like you’re freaking out, before you reach for your phone, before you say a word, stop and count down from 10 to one. Taking even a few seconds before you choose any action gives your logical brain a chance to catch up with your emotions. Once that happens, you’ll find it easier to relax, feel in control, and let some of your anxiety go.

2. Put Your Anxiety to Work

Anxiety in small doses can be a good thing. For example, anxiety about getting in an accident may cause you to drive more cautiously and attentively. Or anxiety about doing poorly on a test may spur you to study an extra half-hour.

But when you feel your anxiety becoming too much, it’s OK to confront it and say out loud, This feeling is unhelpful. I am going to take an action instead.

Writing down how you’re feeling and how you hope to resolve the problem is one example of a helpful action. Putting words on paper or typing them into your phone helps get your emotions out, and it helps give you a sense of control over your situation.

3. Breathe a Box

The history of people using deliberate breathing to control how they feel is almost as old as the history of humankind. It’s also the reason you’ve probably been told to “take a deep breath” at some point when you were angry or upset. You can use this tool to help you relax. The trick is to “breathe a box” using four steps:

  • Inhale through your nose while you silently count to four.
  • Hold that breath while you silently count to four again.
  • Exhale through your mouth for another count of four.
  • Hold your breath for a final count of four.

Inhale for four, hold for four, exhale for four, and hold for four. Repeat this breathing pattern four times. The act of slow, measured breathing tells your body and your brain that you are OK, and it can help calm your anxiety.

4. Imagine Letting Your Anxiety Go

Imagine building a sandcastle on a beach beside the ocean. As you build, take your worries, one at a time, and put them into the structure of your castle. Put them in the floors and walls, naming them as you build. Once the castle is done, take a step back and imagine the waves coming up and washing the castle and the worries out to sea.

When you find this (or any other image) helpful, make a practice of spending a few minutes doing it each day. The more you use a calming image, the easier it will become for you to relax when you think of it.

5. Give Your Worries Away

In Guatemala, children are given small worry dolls. At night, they tell their dolls about what’s bothering them, and then place the dolls under their pillows. In the morning, many children wake up with new ideas about how to solve their problems—thanks to their worry dolls.

Is there something like a worry doll that would work in your life? Some of my patients have used “worry boxes” into which they put slips of paper with their concerns written on them before they go to sleep. Some make a memo on their phone and then revisit it in the morning. Some include their worries in their prayers—giving them over to a higher power.

Research tells us that deliberately setting your worries aside overnight by any of these methods improves your ability to sleep and helps you problem-solve (Scullin et al., 2018).

6. Ask Your Subconscious

Sometimes we become anxious without being able to identify what is bothering us. In those situations, you can interact with your subconscious. Find a calm, quiet place, close your eyes, breathe deeply, and ask the question, What is causing my anxiety? Tune in to what your inner wisdom is telling you.

7. Will It Matter in a Year?

You can gain perspective about the causes of your anxiety by considering how they might impact you in the long-term. Ask yourself, Will this matter in a year?

If not, imagine how an older, wiser you might help you find calm and reassurance right now. What would that conversation sound like? This simple exercise can help separate small issues from ones that deserve more of your energy, attention and focus.

8. Change the Scene

One of the most effective tools against anxiety is changing your sensory input. Step outside. Kick off your shoes. Stand up and stretch. Listen to music. Close your eyes.

Choose an action that interrupts what you are seeing, hearing, touching, smelling or tasting, and that will help you reduce your anxious feelings.

9. Meet the Moment

Avoiding the cause of your anxiety can help relieve it temporarily, but it usually makes things worse in the long run. It’s important to deal with whatever causes your anxiety rather than ignoring or avoiding it.

Facing your anxiety doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing confrontation—you can take small steps toward dealing with situations that intimidate you. Those accomplishments will add up and give you confidence to do more.

10. Go to Your Relaxing Place

Use imagery to help you relax anywhere and anytime. Remember to practice regularly during times when you are calm—that’ll make you an expert at using relaxation techniques when you need them most.

11. Trust Yourself

Sometimes, anxiety is caused by fear of the many possible things that could go wrong in the future. In such cases, it is worthwhile recalling author Mark Twain’s observation, “I have had a lot of worries in my life, most of which never happened.”

As an alternative to thinking of all the unlikely things that could go wrong, calm yourself by recognizing that you can handle much of what might come your way, and if necessary, you can always ask for help.

Takeaway

With practice, including through regularly using some of the tools discussed in this post, anxiety can often be brought under control. Persistent anxiety, or anxiety that interferes with work, sleep, or daily life, warrants talking to a doctor or counselor. Therapy is usually the first-line treatment, but occasionally the addition of anti-anxiety medications is appropriate.
